usage: Polite; the standard line when a beauty-shop clerk offers help
반말, only with a friend, not to staff
I'd like to look on my own
Gently signals you don't need to be followed
examples: 구경 좀 할게요.
I'm just looking.
Said the moment a clerk approaches and asks 뭐 찾으세요?
네, 그냥 구경 좀 할게요. 필요하면 부를게요.
Yeah, just looking — I'll call you if I need help.
부를게요 ('I'll call you') politely sends them off
아직 안 정했어요. 혼자 좀 둘러볼게요.
I haven't decided yet — I'll just browse on my own.

english: Can I try this on (apply a sample)?
usage: Polite; asking to test a sample on your skin
반말, with a friend, not staff
Can I try it on the back of my hand?
손등 ('back of the hand') = where you swatch makeup

Can I try this on?
Pointing at a tester lipstick or cream
립스틱 색 보려고요. 손등에 발라봐도 돼요?
I want to see the lipstick color — can I swatch it on my hand?
손등 is the normal place to test color in Korea
이 선크림 끈적이는지 발라봐도 돼요?
Can I try this sunscreen to see if it's sticky?
끈적이다 ('to be sticky/tacky') names what you're checking

('is it okay to…?'), so 'is it okay if I try applying this?' — the go-to for testing a tester (테스터) cream, lotion, or lipstick. 바르다 is the specific verb for spreading skincare or makeup ON skin (cream, sunscreen, lip balm); it is NOT 칠하다 ('to paint/coat', for walls or nails-as-paint) — using 칠하다 for face cream sounds like you're painting yourself. usage: Polite; the everyday ask at any beauty counter
Could I get a few more samples?
Add 더 ('more') when they give you one or two
Could you throw in some samples?
챙기다 ('to gather/pack for someone') sounds natural and warm
Slightly more tentative; asks if it's possible at all
examples: 샘플 좀 주세요.
Could I get some samples?
Said at checkout after buying something
이거 살게요. 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요.
I'll take this — could you throw in some samples?

혹시 이 크림 샘플 있으면 좀 주세요. 먼저 써보고 싶어서요.

써보고 싶다 ('want to try using') gives a polite reason

Sampling culture is huge in Korea — beauty staff routinely tuck free 샘플 (sachets) into your bag, especially after a purchase, so this is a normal, expected request, not begging. The warm insider version uses 챙기다 ('gather and pack thoughtfully for someone'): 샘플 좀 챙겨 주세요 sounds friendlier than the plain 주세요. usage: Polite; telling staff your skin type
지성 = oily; swap in for your type
민감성 ('sensitive') + 라서요 to explain a need
examples: 저 피부가 건성이에요.
My skin is dry.
Said when a clerk asks 피부 타입이 어떻게 되세요?
저 건성이라 보습되는 거 찾아요.
I have dry skin, so I'm looking for something moisturizing.
건성이라 ('since I'm dry') leads into what you want
여름엔 지성인데 겨울엔 건성이에요. 복합성인가 봐요.
I'm oily in summer but dry in winter — I guess I'm combination.
Describing how your skin shifts by season
nuance: 저 피부가 건성이에요 is 저 ('I', humble) + 피부 ('skin') + 가 (subject particle) + 건성 ('dry type', Sino-Korean 乾性) + 이에요 (polite copula). Korean names skin types with the -성 ('-type/-natured') suffix: 건성 (dry), 지성 (oily), 복합성 (combination), 민감성 (sensitive), 중성 (normal). These are the exact words beauty staff use when asking 피부 타입이 어떻게 되세요?. The crucial point: 건성 is the SKIN-TYPE noun, while 건조하다 is the ADJECTIVE 'to be dry' for a condition right now (건조해요 = 'it feels dry'). So your constitutional type is 건성이에요, but if your skin feels parched today you'd say 피부가 건조해요 — mixing them (저 건조성이에요) is wrong; the type word is 건성, not 건조성. The English-speaker error is translating 'dry skin' literally as 마른 피부 — 마르다 means 'thin/skinny (body)' or 'dried out (laundry)', not skin type; never say 마른 피부 for 건성. usage: What skin type is this for?
Polite; asking which skin a product suits
-용 ('for use by') checks a specific type fast
Can oily skin use this too?
도 ('also') asks if your type is included
examples: 이거 무슨 타입이에요?
What skin type is this for?
Holding a cream, unsure if it fits you
저 지성인데 이거 지성용이에요?
I'm oily — is this for oily skin?
State your type, then check with -용
이 토너 민감성 피부에 써도 괜찮아요?
Is this toner okay for sensitive skin?
괜찮아요 ('is it okay') softens a safety question
nuance: 이거 무슨 타입이에요? is 이거 ('this') + 무슨 ('what kind of') + 타입 (loanword 'type') + 이에요?, asking which skin type a product targets. The most efficient real-shop phrasing, though, uses the suffix -용 ('for the use of'): 건성용 ('for dry skin'), 지성용 ('for oily'), 민감성용 ('for sensitive') — so 이거 건성용이에요? ('is this the dry-skin one?') gets a yes/no instantly. The dividing line: 무슨 타입이에요? is open-ended ('what type?'), while -용이에요? pins down YOUR type. A subtle point: 무슨 vs. 어떤 — 무슨 asks 'what kind/which category', 어떤 asks 'what's it like / which one', and both work here, but 무슨 타입 is the set collocation. The English-speaker error is asking 'what is this for?' as 이거 뭐에 써요? — that asks the product's PURPOSE ('what do you use it for?', e.g. face vs. body), not which skin type; to ask about skin type, say 무슨 타입이에요? or 무슨 피부용이에요?. english: Do you have something really moisturizing?
usage: Polite; asking for a hydrating product
촉촉하다 ('moist, dewy') — the feel you want
속건조 = 'inner dryness' under an oily surface
examples: 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요?
Do you have something moisturizing?
Said when your skin feels tight and dry
겨울이라 너무 당겨요. 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요?
It's winter and my skin feels so tight — anything really moisturizing?
당기다 ('to feel tight/taut') is the dry-skin sensation
저 지성인데 속건조가 심해요. 촉촉하면서 안 무거운 거 추천해 주세요.
I'm oily but really dehydrated underneath — something hydrating but not heavy, please.
The classic '기름지지만 속건조' combination request
nuance: 보습 잘 되는 거 있어요? is 보습 ('moisture retention', Sino-Korean 保濕) + 잘 되는 ('that works well') + 거 ('thing') + 있어요? ('do you have?'). 보습 is THE beauty word for hydration/moisturizing; the product quality is 보습력 ('moisturizing power'), and the sensory result is 촉촉하다 ('dewy, moist'). A key real-life concept is 속건조 ('inner dryness') — skin that's oily on the surface but parched underneath, an extremely common Korean complaint you can name to get the right product. The opposite sensation, 당기다 ('to feel tight/taut'), signals dryness ('당겨요' = 'my skin feels tight'). The English-speaker error is reaching for 수분 vs. 보습 carelessly: 수분 is 'water/moisture (the substance)' and 수분 크림 ('moisture/water cream') is a real category, but to ask generally for 'moisturizing', 보습 잘 되는 거 is the natural request. Another trap is translating 'moist' as 젖은 ('wet, soggy') — that sounds gross for skin; the right word is 촉촉하다. Default 존댓말; the whole frame …는 거 있어요? is the all-purpose 'do you have something that…'.

usage: Polite, full formal term for sunscreen

Not the cream — do you have a sun stick?
선스틱 ('sun stick') for the twist-up format
examples: 선크림 어디 있어요?
Where's the sunscreen?
Asking a clerk to point you to the shelf
얼굴에 바르는 선크림 찾는데 어디 있어요?
I'm looking for facial sunscreen — where is it?
얼굴에 바르는 ('the kind for the face') narrows it
에스피에프 높은 선크림 있어요? 바닷가 가서요.
Do you have high-SPF sunscreen? I'm going to the beach.
